prompt: The Catalogue team says it is perfectly able to build better search. Why does the lesson treat that as the wrong first question?
hint: Able to build it, and…

choices.text: Because the team has overestimated its own skill at search
choices.why: The lesson grants that the team is good and the problem solved; skill is not in doubt.

choices.text: It says nothing about what building would cost
choices.why: Right: capability is one fact, and the decision is about cost and the best use of the hours.

choices.text: Because full-text search is too hard for a product team to own
choices.why: The lesson calls full-text search a solved problem; difficulty is not the objection.

choices.text: Because product asked for it, so product should pick the option
choices.why: Who asked does not change which option is cheaper or which deserves the team's hours.

prompt: Buying search costs Coreto a licence of R$ 9,000 a month, 240 hours of integration in year 1, and a twentieth of an engineer-year (R$ 264,000) to look after it. What does buying cost in year 1, in reais?
Match each option to the trade the lesson says it makes.
hint: What does each one pay with, and what does it get?

pairs.right: Operation for control of the code

right_distractors: Control for a lower first-year price

prompt: Why does the lesson warn against comparing the three options on their year-1 figures?
hint: When does each option spend?

choices.text: Year 1 figures are estimates, while the later years are known costs
choices.why: Later years are estimates too. The problem is the timing of the spending, not the certainty.

choices.text: Year 1 includes one-off work that should be left out
choices.why: The one-off work is a real cost and belongs in the comparison; leaving it out would flatter building.

choices.text: The options spend at different times; year 1 sees the start
choices.why: Right: build front-loads, buy's bill rises, adopt pays in people each year. One year sees only the start.

choices.text: A vendor's first-year price is a discount
choices.why: Coreto's vendor raises the price 10% a year by contract; there is no discount in the example.

prompt: In Geoffrey Moore's sense, what makes an activity core?
hint: Why would a customer pick you over a competitor?

choices.text: It wins customers away from its competitors
choices.why: Right: core is what differentiates. Context is the rest, however much of it has to work.

choices.text: The company would stop if it failed for a day
choices.why: That describes critical work. Payroll is critical and it is context at every company.

choices.text: The engineering team knows how to build it well
choices.why: Skill to build says nothing about whether customers choose you for it.

choices.text: It costs more than a tenth of the budget
choices.why: Size of spend is not the test; a large cost can be pure context.

prompt: Work a company has to do well, but that wins no customer over when it is done well, is what Moore calls ___.
hint: The opposite of core.

prompt: Which of these are core for Coreto, by the lesson's reasoning? Choose all that apply.
hint: Would a theatre leave over it?

choices.text: The seat-hold path during a big on-sale
choices.why: Yes: an on-sale that collapses at 10:00 is exactly what makes a venue leave.

choices.text: The search box on the event pages
choices.why: Critical, but no venue picks a platform for its search, and a vendor sells the same search to competitors.

choices.text: Ticket scanning at the door
choices.why: Yes: a door that fails is a venue's worst night, and a reason to change supplier.

choices.text: Paying Coreto's own staff on time
choices.why: Critical inside Coreto, and invisible to a venue choosing a ticketing platform.

prompt: A year from now Coreto changes strategy: it will win venues by recommending the next show to each buyer. What does the lesson say happens to the search decision?
hint: Whose is the classification?

choices.text: Nothing, since a hosted service is already signed for three years
choices.why: A signed contract does not fix the classification; the strategy does, and it just changed.

choices.text: Search moves towards core, and building is back on the table
choices.why: Right: the classification belongs to the strategy, so a new strategy reopens it.

choices.text: Search stays context, because it was classified as context at the time
choices.why: Core moves. A classification frozen at the first decision ignores what changed.

choices.text: Coreto should adopt open source to keep options open
choices.why: Adopting makes Coreto an operator; if ranking becomes core, the question is whether to build it.

prompt: Over three years, building search costs R$ 450,000 and buying it costs R$ 433,080. How much cheaper is buying, in reais?
Put the three options in order of three-year total, cheapest first.
hint: Column E, not column B.
trap: Ordering by year 1 puts adopt (R$ 241,200) ahead of build (R$ 246,000). Over three years build's flat R$ 102,000 a year puts it well ahead of adopt.

prompt: Why does the sheet find the cheapest option with INDEX and MATCH rather than by reading the column and typing the name?
hint: What happens when somebody edits a number?

choices.text: It is the only way to compare text in a spreadsheet
choices.why: Nothing here compares text; MIN compares numbers and INDEX fetches a name.

choices.text: The answer follows the numbers when they change
choices.why: Right: MATCH finds the position of the smallest total and INDEX returns the name there, so an edited estimate updates the verdict.

choices.text: A typed name would round the totals
choices.why: Typing a name in another cell does not touch the totals at all.

choices.text: MATCH also checks that the estimates are realistic
choices.why: MATCH finds a position. Whether 960 hours is realistic is a judgement no formula makes.

prompt: Davi's director asks to see the comparison over four years instead of three. Using the lesson's arithmetic, what changes?
hint: The licence rises 10% again; build's running cost does not.

choices.text: Building becomes the cheapest, R$ 552,000 against buying's R$ 590,028
choices.why: Right: year 4 adds R$ 102,000 to building and R$ 156,948 to buying, which overturns a lead of R$ 16,920.

choices.text: Buying stays the cheapest, by a wider margin
choices.why: The margin shrank each year already; a fourth year with a dearer licence reverses it.

choices.text: Adopting becomes the cheapest
choices.why: Adopt costs R$ 169,200 a year from year 2, more than either of the others; a longer horizon makes it worse.

choices.text: Nothing, because year 4 costs the same as year 3
choices.why: Buy's year 4 is dearer than its year 3, since the contract raises the licence again.

prompt: Buying beats building by R$ 16,920 over three years. What does the lesson make of that margin?
hint: Compare it with the build estimate in hours.

choices.text: It is a clear win for buying, and the decision is made
choices.why: About 113 engineer-hours against a 960-hour estimate is inside the error of the estimate itself.

choices.text: The money does not decide it
choices.why: Right: a 12% overrun on the build would erase it, so the unpriced items do the deciding.

choices.text: Building should be chosen, to avoid paying a vendor
choices.why: Avoiding a vendor is a preference, and the sheet already says building costs more over three years.

choices.text: The estimates should be redone until one option wins clearly
choices.why: Re-estimating until a clear winner appears is tuning the answer, not finding it.

prompt: Adopting an open-source engine pays no licence, yet it is Coreto's most expensive option. Where does the money go?
hint: Look at the people column.

choices.text: Into a paid support contract with the project
choices.why: Coreto's estimate has no support contract; the cost is its own people.

choices.text: Into people who operate and upgrade it
choices.why: Right: R$ 273,600 over three years is people, the largest people line of the three options.

choices.text: Into a fee for the commercial licence
choices.why: The example pays no licence at all for the engine.

choices.text: Into rewriting the engine for Coreto
choices.why: Nobody rewrites the engine; changing it is a reason to adopt that the lesson says Coreto does not have.

prompt: Adopting costs Coreto 30% of an engineer-year (R$ 264,000) to operate the engine and 80 hours a year of upgrades at R$ 150. What is adopt's people cost per year, in reais?
The company behind the engine you run moves it to a new licence. By the lesson, what happens?
hint: The versions you already have, and the ones to come.

choices.text: Your running copy becomes illegal overnight
choices.why: By the lesson, a licence change applies to new releases; copies already released keep the licence they came with.

choices.text: Old versions keep their licence, and each way forward costs
choices.why: Right: stay on an old version, move to another project, or pay. Each answer has a price the original sheet did not hold.

choices.text: The new terms apply to companies larger than Coreto, so it is exempt
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about company size; the question is whether the new terms fit how you use it.

choices.text: A self-hosted user is unaffected, since the code is already in hand
choices.why: Self-hosting is exactly the case where the next upgrade brings the new terms with it.

prompt: Another company like Coreto has a platform team that already runs the same open-source engine for its logs. Which line of its search sheet changes most?
hint: Which work would already be happening?

choices.text: The licence line, which falls to zero
choices.why: The licence was zero already; that is not where adopting costs money.

choices.text: The buy option's licence, which the vendor decides to lower
choices.why: Nothing about another team's engine moves a vendor's price.

choices.text: Adopt's operation and upgrades, now shared
choices.why: Right: the people line was adopt's largest, and an existing operator absorbs much of it.

choices.text: Build's one-off hours, which shrink
choices.why: The engine running for logs does not write Postgres search for anybody.

prompt: A staff engineer proposes building Coreto's own expense-report tool for its employees, because the engineers could make one nicer than any on the market. Which test from the lesson settles it fastest?
hint: Who chooses Coreto, and why?

choices.text: Would a venue leave Coreto over it?
choices.why: Right: no venue knows or cares, so it is context, and a nicer version is hours core does not get.

choices.text: A three-year sheet of build, buy and adopt
choices.why: The sheet would help later; the core question answers this before any sum is needed.

choices.text: Asking whether the team is able to build it
choices.why: That is the first question the lesson calls wrong: being able says nothing about being worth it.

choices.text: Checking whether an open-source tool exists
choices.why: An open-source option is one of three, and adopting has costs of its own; it does not settle the classification.

prompt: Carried to four years, Coreto's search sheet makes ___ the cheapest option.
hint: The option whose running cost does not rise.

prompt: Which of these things left out of the three-year sheet lean against building? Choose all that apply.
hint: The database, and the hours.

choices.text: Search load on the database holding the seat locks
choices.why: Yes: an on-sale is when buyers search hardest, on the path the strategy protects.

choices.text: What leaving the vendor would cost
choices.why: That leans against buying; lesson 9 prices it.

choices.text: What the 960 hours would have done on the reservation path
choices.why: Yes: an opportunity cost, which lesson 13 prices.

choices.text: How soon buyers get better search
choices.why: That favours buying, whose integration is 240 hours against 960.

prompt: Davi's note recommends buying, then adds two things to do before signing. Which pair is it?
hint: One is about leaving, one about the price.

choices.text: Run a pilot with the open-source engine, and hire a search specialist
choices.why: Adopting was rejected in the same note; a pilot of it is not among the conditions.

choices.text: Price what leaving would cost, and get the yearly rise capped
choices.why: Right: the exit leans against buying, and the uncapped 10% rise is what makes building cheaper by year 4.

choices.text: Get a discount on year 1, and move search to the reservation database
choices.why: Year 1 is already the cheapest; moving search onto that database is the risk the note avoids.

choices.text: Ask product to drop typo tolerance, and sign for three years
choices.why: Typo tolerance is what Júlia asked for; dropping it would not answer her request.
